It remains identical with itself because its original “nature” determines its negation, and that negation in turn determines the result. Yet it is also different from the “given” nature that it originally was, because the result it has become is the negation of that first nature.
In other words, once the dialectical entity has become synthetic or total, it has remained itself: it is itself changing itself.

And it is only by changing itself that it has truly become itself. It is nothing other than this dialectical transformation of what it is. It has become—or, if you prefer, remained—itself precisely because it has not remained the same.

So a dialectical entity must always be described as a result, a totality, or a synthesis—that is, under its synthetic aspect. It must be described not as something merely “given,” but as something “produced”: something that has produced itself by negating what was given to it.

At the very least, any adequate description must include this aspect and end with it—unless the synthesis in question turns out to be a new thesis. But we must never describe a synthesis without first describing the corresponding thesis and antithesis.

For a reader encountering dialectic for the first time, everything just said will no doubt seem unconvincing, arbitrary, and artificial. And in fact, no merely formal and abstract definition of dialectic can be convincing. What can convince us is only a concrete description of dialectic actually being realized.
But the only true realization of dialectic is human or historical existence. So to speak convincingly about dialectic is ultimately to speak about human existence.

The system as a whole describes this existence from its different sides, and its phenomenological side is dealt with above all by the Phenomenology. Only the actual text of the Phenomenology can therefore make the reader see, to some extent, why the abstract claims made above about the dialectical form of existence are correct.

Only by reaching the end of the book will the meaning of terms such as “identity,” “negativity,” and “totality”; “thesis,” “antithesis,” and “synthesis”; “dialectical sublation” and “mediation”; “dialectical movement,” “becoming,” and “result”; the “circularity” of the dialectical entity; and so on, become fully clear.
Still, to make the book easier to understand, we should already say a few words about real dialectic.
As I have said many times already, if dialectic is realized only in human beings, then human beings are specifically human—that is, distinct from animals—only insofar as they are dialectical.
So we can fully understand the human being only if we understand what dialectic is. And conversely, we can fully understand dialectic only if we understand the human being.
To make our abstract discussion of dialectic more intelligible, then, we must supplement it with at least a brief description of the human being as the entity in which dialectic is realized.

If we say that human beings really do realize dialectic—that they really are dialectical beings—then we must also say that they are not wholly or merely “identical.” They are not always and everywhere equal to themselves, simply being what they are.
They must change, and they must change essentially. More than that, they themselves must be the cause of these essential changes.
Since a human being is dialectical as a human being rather than as a natural “thing” or an animal, what must change is precisely their human “essence” or “nature.”

It is therefore better to say that there is no fixed human “essence” or “nature” at all, and that what distinguishes human beings from every natural “thing” is precisely the absence of any eternal and unchanging human nature.
This dialectical view of humanity is at once extremely ancient and entirely new.

It reaches back to the earliest times and appears in all “primitive” or “magical” views of the world, according to which a human being could, under certain conditions, transform himself into whatever he wished: a stone, a blade of grass, an animal, another human being, a “god,” and so on.

But the “magical” worldview did not distinguish between the animal or bodily side of human existence and its specifically human or “spiritual” side. It assumed that both could undergo essential transformation.
Since this is plainly false of the natural side, people eventually noticed the mistake and abandoned magic. But in doing so, they also abandoned the “magical”—that is, dialectical—view of humanity.
This, at least, is what the Greeks did.

They too made no essential distinction between what is natural and what is human. So once they had discovered the category of identity, they applied it equally to both. This gave rise, in science and philosophy, to a non-dialectical picture of the human being as a kind of “thing” possessing an eternal and unchanging “nature” or “essence.”
This conception survived all the way to Hegel, and it still survives in the “science” of humanity—at least in bourgeois science.

Alongside this scientific and philosophical conception, however, there was another view, and it still exists. Its source is the Bible, and it is characteristic of Jewish and Christian religious thought.
This conception is dialectical insofar as it recognizes that a human being can change his own human “nature” or “essence.” We see this in the idea of conversion, whether in Judaism or Christianity.

From the point of view of these religions, the difference between a Gentile and a Jew, or between a pagan or Jew and a Christian, is essential in every sense of the word. Yet a pagan can himself become—can make himself—a Christian while still remaining the same individual, and so on.

But this religious idea of “conversion,” of an “essential transformation,” is very closely tied to the idea of “God” or of an all-powerful being—a being which, incidentally, is “identical,” at least in Jewish and Christian theologies built on Greek science.
So in the end—in practice, if not always in words—the religious conception preserved the principle of essential change but gave up the idea that the human being himself brings this change about.
A person can change essentially only because “God” wills it: it is a matter of “grace,” and so on.
For this reason, the religious conception cannot be regarded as fully dialectical. To make it so, we must strip away its theological shell.
And this, in practice if not always explicitly, was accomplished by the movement of thought we call Romanticism.
A “Romantic” view can and should be regarded as a Jewish-Christian conception. But we must immediately add that it removes everything that binds the human being to God.

So if a Romantic changes essentially, it is because he himself changes himself. Nothing and no one can prevent him from doing so. He therefore stands, so to speak, on intimate terms with God—and this is the Romantic “theomachy,” the struggle with God.
In practice, the Romantic conception of humanity is therefore atheistic.
And this atheistic-Christian view of humanity can rightly be called dialectical.
In any case, there can be no doubt that Hegel’s dialectical anthropology has its immediate roots in Romanticism.

But we should not imagine that Hegel was simply one of the Romantics, or that he had nothing fundamentally new to say about humanity. In fact, he advanced this line of thought enormously. From a philosophical point of view, the relation between Hegel and Romanticism can be compared only to the relation between an acorn and a hundred-year-old oak.

Hegel did more than finally understand something no Romantic had ever fully and clearly explained: that the Romantic or dialectical conception of humanity necessarily includes, or presupposes, radical atheism.
He did more than give the clear and precise form of the concept to what, in the Romantics, had remained vague aesthetic “images” and obscure literary “ideas.”
He was also the first to recognize something in dialectic and dialectical anthropology that no Romantic had noticed: physical work and bloody struggle.
The Romantics imagined that it was the “poet,” the “painter,” or more generally the individual living an intense “inner life” who could change himself essentially.
And although Romantic “heroes” acted and struggled, they never worked.

Their struggles were therefore not the cause of their transformation. They were only the outward—and fundamentally contingent, even accidental—expression of a transformation occurring entirely “within.”
Hegel, by contrast, understood that human beings change essentially only insofar as they take part in real work and real struggle.

Once he saw this, he also saw why the strictly Romantic “hero”—ultimately an idle and unproductive figure—is inevitably condemned to failure, death, suicide, or, as so often happened to the Romantics themselves, the melancholy of the mal du siècle, born of being “misunderstood” and “unrecognized.”

Once we make this correction—once we recognize that “Romantic” existence is not realized by the Romantic writer, nor within the pages of his books, but in real historical life, and therefore, in our own time and ultimately, in the USSR—we can still say that the dialectical conception of humanity is Romantic at its root.
So if we want to give the reader a preliminary concept—or rather, a broad “image”—of the dialectical human being, the best references are Goethe’s Faust, Byron’s heroes, Lermontov’s Demon, and so on.
If we isolate and develop the philosophical—and dialectical—concepts underlying all these Romantic “images,” then the first thing we must say is this.
If the Romantic-dialectical human being is above all a being who is essentially changing, then human existence belongs first of all to time, rather than to space.

Of course, a natural “thing” also exists in time, as everything that exists does. But just as time matters far more to moving things than to motionless ones, time is far more essential to human existence than to natural existence.
We can say of nature that it exists also in time. But of humanity it would be more accurate to say that it exists also in space, while existing first and foremost in time.
Human beings and natural things exist in one and the same spatial world, in one and the same space.
But what exists in space is only what has either “always existed” or has “already been made.” And, as we will soon see, this is precisely what is non-human—or non-dialectical—in humanity.
The making, the change itself, takes place as though outside space, in time.
And it is precisely time that constitutes properly human existence.
Natural “things” certainly change too, and so they too are “in time.” But their changes are not essential. Their being in time is therefore not essential to what they are.
For human beings, the opposite is true.
In one sense, of course, natural things and human beings exist in the same time. A thing can exist at the same time as a person, or before that person, or after them.
But, as we will see again, the “natural” time in which things endure and change is not quite the same as the “historical” time in which human beings exist.
Natural time can be understood as simply the fourth dimension of space, and this is precisely how contemporary physics uses it: as a fourth, imaginary dimension of space.

In that sense, it resembles space. If we know its “present,” we thereby know its entire past and future. The temporal extension of a natural “thing” can be taken in at a “single glance” just as its spatial extension can.
In historical time, by contrast, prediction of this kind is impossible. Something genuinely happens there, and to know what happens we must wait for it to happen.
Historical time is therefore not merely unlike space. It is, in a sense, opposed to it.
So we can say that space corresponds to “identity” in the same way that historical time corresponds to “negativity.”
By calling human time “historical,” I have already indicated that dialectical existence—which is essentially temporal—can also be defined as historical.
For essential change in human beings and humanity through time is precisely what we call history in the proper sense of the word.

And insofar as genuinely new forms of human existence arise during the historical process—forms that are not merely different from those that came before them, but opposed to them, that is, forms which “negate” them—history is nothing other than a succession of revolutions, in the broad sense of the word.
Dialectical existence, then—existence that is essentially temporal or historical—is always also revolutionary.
And to say “revolution” is already to say freedom.

Revolutions in the proper sense have always been carried out in the name of human “freedom.” It is therefore clear that only free people—that is, people who actively and effectively strive for freedom, rather than people content with slavery—can make revolutions.
And we will see not only that there can be no revolution without freedom, but also that there can be no freedom outside revolution or without it.
For freedom is nothing other than negativity.
It is not, as people usually think, a “choice” between two things already given. It is the negation of what is given—a real and effective negation.
So the Romantic-dialectical existence of the human being, being essentially temporal, is always historical; therefore revolutionary; therefore free.
And, as we will have occasion to discuss again, human freedom necessarily presupposes—and partly expresses and realizes—the essential finitude of the human being: that is, human mortality.
We therefore arrive again at Hegel’s claim that only the finite determinations of an entity can be “dialectically sublated.”
In other words, a human being can be dialectical—historical, revolutionary, or free—only because he is mortal.
In this sense, then, we can say that negativity corresponds, in a certain way, to death.
At first sight, this claim is not especially convincing.
And in fact, only the Phenomenology as a whole can make it fully convincing—that is, can truly prove it. We will return to the question later in this “introduction.”

For now, it is enough to point out that if we do not assume human mortality, it becomes difficult to see how a revolution could ever succeed, how freedom could ever be realized, or even how history itself could exist—that is, how human beings and humanity could undergo essential change through time.

Suppose a particular balance of forces allowed one class to dominate another, and the members of the dominant class were immortal. It would then be impossible to see how or why this balance could ever change.
They would never leave historical reality of their own accord, and no one could “remove” them from it. Remaining there forever, they would enjoy forever the advantages history had given them.
In the most literal sense, what meaning would there be in demanding “your money or your life”—a demand that ultimately lies behind every genuine revolution—from immortal people?
Let us accept, then, that the human being who realizes dialectic must necessarily be finite—that is, mortal.
Two extremely important and necessary conclusions follow.

First, by accepting the finitude or absolute death of the human being—that is, by denying the existence within him of some immortal “soul”—we bind him finally and irreversibly to his body, and through his body to the entire natural world.
There can be no dialectical human being before, after, or outside the body, just as there can be no human being before, after, or outside the natural world: the spatial, temporal, material world.
